cands.bio: U.S. Representative for California's 35th District since 2015. Born in Guatemala. Worked 17 years as an LAPD 911 dispatcher. Pomona City Council member 2000–2006 and mayor 2006–2008. Served in the California Assembly 2008–2013 and the State Senate 2013–2014. Sits on the House Appropriations Committee.

endorsements.text: Democratic Party of California (2026 general election)
California Federation of Labor Unions, AFL-CIO (2026)
Planned Parenthood of Orange and San Bernardino Counties' Community Action Fund (2026)

cands.gaps: We could not find where Torres grew up, her birth city, or the year she first came to the United States. We found no statements or actions from her on data centers, homestead property taxes, limits on investor or foreign land buying, growth and land protection, police pay, gun laws, abortion, or school choice and teacher pay. Her campaign site's issue pages (housing, environment, women's rights and others) were not readable, only their titles. The Ballotpedia page we had was cut off partway through the 117th Congress, so earlier votes and the state legislative record were not read. She did not complete Ballotpedia's candidate survey.

votes.what: Final FY2026 spending package funding most remaining federal agencies through September 30, 2026.

votes.bill: S. 1071 / FY2026 National Defense Authorization Act (final)
votes.what: Final FY2026 defense policy and funding-authorization bill (about $900 billion), carried in the House on the vehicle S. 1071.

votes.bill: H.R. 5371 (2025) Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2026 (Nov. 12 final, ended the shutdown)
votes.what: Ended the 43-day federal shutdown: funds government through Jan. 30, 2026 and three full-year spending bills.

votes.bill: H.R. 5371 (2025) Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2026 (Sept. 19 House passage)
votes.what: House-passed stopgap funding bill to keep government open through Nov. 21, 2025; stalled in the Senate and a shutdown began Oct. 1.

votes.bill: H.R. 1 (2025) One Big Beautiful Bill Act (final passage)
votes.what: The 2025 reconciliation law: extends the 2017 tax cuts, adds new tax breaks, cuts Medicaid and food-assistance spending, and raises defense and border spending and the debt limit.

votes.bill: H.R. 881 (2025) DHS Restrictions on Confucius Institutes and Chinese Entities of Concern Act
votes.what: Bars Homeland Security funds going to Confucius Institutes and entities tied to the Chinese government.
Requires documentary proof of U.S. citizenship to register to vote in federal elections.

votes.bill: H.R. 1968 (2025) Full-Year Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2025
votes.what: Funds the federal government through September 30, 2025 at roughly prior-year levels (March 2025 stopgap).

votes.bill: H.R. 152 (2025) Federal Disaster Assistance Coordination Act
votes.what: Streamlines coordination among federal agencies delivering disaster aid (hurricane/flood recovery).
Requires federal detention of undocumented immigrants charged with theft, burglary or assault of a police officer, and lets states sue over immigration enforcement.

cands.name: Mike Cargile

money.note: Individuals gave $9,799; PAC money $0; candidate's own money $0. Percentages describe itemized individual gifts, which the FEC has processed through about July 2026.

cands.bio: Filmmaker and president of Big Event Pictures. Served in the U.S. Army 1990–91 and moved to California in 1991. Has worked as a writer, producer and marketing director. Republican nominee for California's 35th District in 2020, 2022, 2024 and 2026. No elected office listed.

endorsements.text: 2026: April's Common Sense Cali Voters, a voter-guide group, per Ballotpedia.

2024, listed by Cargile himself in his Ballotpedia survey: LA GOP, SB GOP, National Right to Life, Moms for Liberty, Crime Victims United, Republican National Hispanic Assembly, CRPA, Howard Jarvis and Pastor Jack Hibbs. Ballotpedia did not independently identify endorsements for that race.

cands.gaps: We could not find where Cargile grew up. Sources give his birthplace as Killeen or Fort Hood, Texas. We found no documented stance or action on data centers, development, growth limits, homestead property taxes, or limits on investor or foreign buyers of homes and land. He has held no office, so there are no official actions to report. Ballotpedia lists a 2020 event in which the California Republican Party removed its endorsement of him, but the page text we had was cut off before any details, so we left it out. His campaign website mentions an election-integrity lawsuit, but we did not see enough detail to report it.

local.label: Roots 55: He says he moved to California in 1991 and has raised his family in Southern California, about 35 years as an adult resident; his birthplace is Texas and where he grew up is not stated.

score.why: Raised $9,799, under $50,000 for this office: too little money to score fairly.

qual.background: Filmmaker, producer and marketing director; short stint as an Army Quartermaster officer (1990–91); school crossing guard, coach and booster club president; he has not held elected office.
qual.why: He has no legislative, executive, legal or policy-office experience, and his career is in film and marketing. He has run for this seat four times without winning, and he says prior government experience is not needed.
qual.label: He has no legislative, executive, legal or policy-office experience, and his career is in film and marketing. He has run for this seat four times without winning, and he says prior government experience is not needed.

clean-money.evidence: His campaign site says it receives no financial support from AIPAC, any political party, super PAC, corporation or special interest group, and is funded solely by "We, the People."

second-amendment.evidence: His campaign site says the right to keep and bear arms "shall not be infringed" and that any restriction, registration or regulation of that right is an unconstitutional infringement.

school-choice-teachers.evidence: His campaign website, as quoted on Ballotpedia, says he is "absolutely pro-choice" on education and wants parents to be able to choose public, online, private, charter or home schools. The excerpt does not mention teacher pay.

back-police-order.evidence: His campaign website, as quoted on Ballotpedia, says he will never support defunding police. It calls for more spending on tactical training, hiring more officers, and student-loan relief for law enforcement.

workers-first.evidence: His campaign site opposes open borders and cites trafficking, fentanyl and lost American jobs. His website plan, quoted on Ballotpedia, calls for completing the border wall and enforcing immigration law, but also a one-time expedited citizenship path for non-citizens who lived here before 2016 and have no felony record.
